name: CAUL-LOW YOUR BLISS BURGER (Served with fried cauliflower)

recipe.history:
Cauliflower's journey from the wild brassica fields of the eastern Mediterranean to the beer batter of American pub kitchens is a story of continuous reinvention. The vegetable was first cultivated in Cyprus and coastal Asia Minor and traveled westward into Europe via Arab traders in the twelfth century. It became a prestige ingredient in the courts of France and Italy before descending into home kitchens across the continent. In the Indian subcontinent, where it arrived via Mughal trade routes, it found its most exuberant culinary expression — fried cauliflower preparations, spiced and battered or simply deep-fried to golden crispness, became part of the everyday Indian street food tradition. Pakoras made with cauliflower florets, dipped in a spiced chickpea batter and fried in ghee or oil, represent one of the oldest known applications of battered fried cauliflower and point to a tradition that long predates European tempura or American beer batter.

Beer-battered cauliflower arrived in American kitchens through the confluence of two trends: the craft beer explosion of the 1990s and 2000s, which made high-quality local ales and lagers available everywhere, and the growing interest in fried vegetable preparations as either meat substitutes or premium side dishes. Pub-style beer batter — made with cold lager or ale, flour, baking powder, and seasoning — creates a coating that is simultaneously light and crunchy, with a subtle malty bitterness that complements rather than overwhelms whatever is inside. Applied to cauliflower florets, beer batter produces something that is crispy on the outside, tender and almost creamy within, and deeply satisfying alongside a beef burger. The combination appeared first in gastropubs in the late 2000s and spread quickly.

I made beer-battered cauliflower for a burger the first time because I was trying to use up a head of cauliflower and a half-can of lager that had gone flat. I made a quick batter, fried the florets in batches in a wide pot of oil, and ate three of them standing over the stove before they even made it to the burger. They were better than any fries I had made in months. I piled the rest on top of a medium-rare patty with a smear of spicy aioli, ate it over the sink because there were no clean plates, and called it one of my better decisions that year.

Cooking the patty for this burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is essential because the beer-battered cauliflower is rich, heavy, and intensely textured. The burger needs a patty that is juicy enough to provide a counterbalancing succulence, a bright beefy richness that cuts through the fried coating and the starchy florets. A well-done patty would turn the whole plate into a dry, heavy exercise. Medium rare provides the moisture and fat that makes the combination sing. The patty is the anchor; the cauliflower is the drama. The anchor must hold.
ingredients: 6 tbsp unsalted butter, softened and cubed
1 medium head cauliflower, cut into bite-sized florets
1 1/4 cups cold lager or pale ale (very cold, from fridge)
Neutral oil for frying (enough to fill pot 3 inches deep)
2 tbsp hot sauce (such as Frank's or Crystal)
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Dissolve yeast in warm milk with 1 tsp sugar; bloom 10 minutes. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine flour, remaining sugar, and salt. Add yeast mixture and eggs; mix on low 3 minutes, then medium. Add butter one cube at a time over 8–10 minutes until dough is smooth and glossy.

2. Refrigerate dough overnight (8–12 hours). Divide into 4 portions (about 120g each), shape into tight rounds, proof at room temperature 2–3 hours until doubled. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C), brush with egg wash, bake 18–20 minutes until deep golden. Cool on rack.
3. Make the spicy aioli: Whisk all ingredients together, adjust heat to preference. Refrigerate.

4. Prepare the beer batter: In a large bowl, whisk together 1 cup flour, baking powder, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, cayenne, and 1 tsp salt. Keep refrigerated. Do not add the beer until just before frying.
5. Dredge station: Place the remaining 1/2 cup flour seasoned with 1/2 tsp salt in a shallow dish. Toss cauliflower florets in the seasoned flour and shake off excess. Set aside.
6. Heat 3 inches of neutral oil in a heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven to 365°F (185°C).
7. Just before frying, whisk the cold beer into the refrigerated batter mixture until just combined — a few lumps are fine and preferred. Do not overmix or the batter will toughen.

8. Working in batches of 6–8 florets, dip each flour-dusted floret into the beer batter, letting excess drip off. Gently lower into the hot oil. Fry 3–4 minutes, turning once, until deeply golden and cooked through. Drain on a wire rack; season immediately with flaky salt. Hold in a 200°F (95°C) oven while frying remaining batches.

9. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into 3/4-inch-thick patties slightly wider than the buns. Press a center dimple. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder.

10. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add oil. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes. Flip once. Lay a slice of cheddar on each. Cook 2–3 more minutes, tenting if needed, until center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C). Rest 3 minutes.
11. Split brioche buns and toast cut-side down in the skillet fat 60–90 seconds.
12. Assemble: Spread spicy aioli on both cut faces of each bun. Place romaine lettuce, tomato, and white onion on the bottom bun; season tomato with flaky salt.
13. Place the cheddar-topped patty on top. Pile 4–6 beer-battered cauliflower florets on top of the patty, pressing gently so they sit.
14. A few drops of malt vinegar on the cauliflower before closing is optional but highly recommended. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately before the batter softens.
